ai.definition: Omega-Point Simulation is a theoretical concept in computing that envisions simulating every possible state and variation of the universe at a microscopic level, effectively creating a digital representation encompassing all historical and potential future events.
ai.howItWorks: The simulation would theoretically achieve this scale by utilizing the entire mass of the galaxy, transforming it into 'computronium', which is an abstract term for matter that has been optimized to serve as computing hardware at the finest granularity. This transformation would enable the processing power necessary to simulate every quantum state and interaction within the universe.
ai.problemSolved: It aims to address the challenge of comprehensively modeling cosmic phenomena, including all historical events and potential future scenarios, which is beyond the capability of current computational technologies.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process for Omega-Point Simulation is purely theoretical. It involves converting the entire observable mass into computronium, a concept that currently lacks physical realization or empirical evidence.
ai.buildProcess: No specific build process exists as it is a theoretical framework. The process would require an unprecedented level of technological advancement and possibly new physics to understand how matter can be transformed into such efficient computing hardware at the quantum scale.
ai.costDrivers: The cost drivers are purely speculative, but they include the energy required for transformation, the physical infrastructure needed, and the advanced technology necessary for such a massive simulation. These factors would make it prohibitively expensive with current knowledge of physics and economics.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook remains in the realm of theoretical research and speculation. It is not expected to enter practical development or commercialization within the foreseeable future due to its extreme requirements.
ai.regulation: There are no current regulations applicable to Omega-Point Simulation as it is purely a theoretical concept with no existing physical manifestation.
ai.risks: The risks include technological limitations, ethical concerns regarding such a massive simulation, and the potential for unforeseen consequences if such a simulation were ever attempted or achieved.
ai.profitability: Not applicable due to its theoretical nature and lack of practical application in current economic contexts.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential future developments could involve advancements in quantum computing, material science, and our understanding of physical laws that might make this concept more feasible. However, these are speculative and far from realization.

glossary.def: A hypothetical form of matter optimized for use as computing hardware at the finest granularity.

A theoretical concept in computing that envisions simulating every possible state and variation of the universe, effectively creating a digital representation encompassing all historical and potential future events.

subsystems.name: Computational substrate
subsystems.role: matter rebuilt so that almost every atom stores and processes information — the idea sometimes called computronium.
parts: paths for waste heat to escape

subsystems.name: Energy and heat management
subsystems.role: supplies power and, crucially, removes the heat of irreversible operations.

subsystems.name: Disassembly and conversion plant
subsystems.role: takes apart planets, moons and eventually stars and rebuilds them into substrate.

subsystems.name: Simulation engine
subsystems.role: the software that evolves a universe model forward from given initial conditions.

subsystems.name: Readout and interpretation
subsystems.role: turns the raw evolved state into histories a user can query.

buildSteps.title: Fix the physical budget
buildSteps.detail: Work out how many bits a given mass and energy can hold and flip, using thermodynamics and relativity. The Landauer limit sets a minimum energy per erased bit; the Bekenstein bound caps how many bits a region of given size and energy can contain.

buildSteps.title: Build reversible logic
buildSteps.detail: Ordinary chips throw away energy on every irreversible operation. Computations that are logically reversible can in principle run far below the Landauer limit, so they are the first hardware target.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate substrate in the lab
buildSteps.detail: Build small devices that compute efficiently at low temperature with extreme error correction, and measure real operation rates against the Margolus–Levitin ceiling on operations per second per joule.

buildSteps.title: Scale to a planet
buildSteps.detail: Convert a body's mass into substrate and power it from a star, which requires dismantling and reassembling matter at a scale no current industry approaches.

buildSteps.title: Capture the star
buildSteps.detail: Orbiting collectors gather most of the star's output — the megastructure concept usually called a Dyson swarm — because a simulation of a cosmos needs energy on that order.

buildSteps.title: Gather initial conditions
buildSteps.detail: No simulation can start from perfect knowledge. You would seed it with measured cosmic data, such as maps of the cosmic microwave background, and run large ensembles of slightly different starting states to cover the uncertainty.

buildSteps.title: Run and error-correct
buildSteps.detail: Evolve the model forward, continuously correcting faults from cosmic rays and thermal noise. Reaching full cosmic history means either enormous time or enormous parallelism.

buildSteps.title: Read out histories
buildSteps.detail: Query the final state for the structures and events of interest, since the point of the exercise is reconstruction rather than raw number-crunching.

prerequisites.why: Landauer's principle, the Bekenstein bound and the Margolus–Levitin theorem give the theoretical energy, density and speed ceilings any such machine must obey.
reversible logic has been demonstrated in the laboratory, but nothing operates close to the Landauer limit at useful scale.
self-replication is well understood in theory and in biology, but machines that build copies of themselves at industrial scale do not exist.
there is no engineering path today to collecting a significant fraction of a star's output.
the classic version of this idea assumes a universe that eventually stops expanding and collapses, concentrating energy and time; measurements of accelerating expansion point the other way.

pathway.milestone: theory only — the limits are calculated, and the Omega Point cosmology has been worked out in book form
pathway.unlocks: a precise statement of what is and is not forbidden by physics.

pathway.milestone: laboratory computing at or near the Landauer limit
pathway.unlocks: evidence that efficiency, not just raw speed, can be pushed to the physical floor.

pathway.milestone: planetary-scale computing and megastructure engineering, if ever feasible
pathway.unlocks: the first substrate large enough to matter cosmologically.

pathway.milestone: galaxy-scale substrate running a cosmos model
pathway.unlocks: the proposed capability — but accelerating cosmic expansion probably forbids the endless collapsing-universe version, so at best a finite, bounded simulation is conceivable.
